title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Introduction
content: The putamen, combined with the globus pallidus, forms the lentiform nucleus. The caudate nucleus shapes the striatum, which is a subcortical structure that forms the basal ganglia (see Image. Putamen and Caudate Nucleus). The putamen is involved in learning and motor control, including speech articulation, language functions, reward, cognitive functioning, and addiction. [1] [2] [3] Research has noted putaminal dysfunctions in various motor and cognitive dysfunctions, namely Parkinson disease, Huntington disease, Alzheimer disease, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, Wilson disease, and autism.

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Structure and Function
content: The basal ganglia are a group of deep-brain nuclei that divide into the putamen, caudate nucleus, nucleus accumbens, and globus pallidus. The putamen, caudate, and nucleus accumbens collectively form the striatum. Different parts of the striatum receive afferent input from different cortical regions and project their efferent output to the cortex through the thalamus. [4] [5] The anterior putamen connects with the associative regions in the cortex, and the posterior portion connects with the primary motor cortex and the supplementary motor area. [4] [6]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Structure and Function
content: The striatum plays a significant role in various brain functions, including motor control and learning, language, reward, cognitive functioning, and addiction through the functional cortico-striato-thalamocortical neural pathways. [3] [7] Traditionally, the basal ganglia structures are known for their motor functions. However, it is well established that the basal ganglia are not only involved in purely motor functions but also associated with more complex goal-directed behaviors, including components of emotion, motivation, and cognition that contribute to the expression of a particular movement. [1] Therefore, a pathologic state (eg, neurodegeneration or hemorrhage) in the striatum can lead to a broad range of clinical manifestations from motor dysfunction such as Parkinson disease to various psychiatric disorders. [3] [8] The putamen is also involved in modulating both sensory and motor aspects of pain. [9]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Embryology
content: From cephalic to caudal, the primary 3 primitive brain vesicles differentiate into the prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), and rhombencephalon (hindbrain). By the end of the fifth week of gestation, the prosencephalon differentiates into the telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres) and the diencephalon (see Image. Horizontal Section of the Right Cerebral Hemisphere). [10] The telencephalon gives rise to most of the components of the basal ganglia, which include the caudate and the putamen. [7] The globus pallidus originates from neuroblasts in the wall of the 3rd ventricle of the diencephalon.

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: The putamen receives its vascular supply from the perforating branches of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA), also known as the lenticulostriate arteries, with variations of the predominance of either ACA or MCA supply. [11] Although the brain tissue with the highest metabolic rate lacks a conventional lymphatic system responsible for cleansing waste, the brain parenchyma has its specific lymphatic drainage pathways, which are composed of: Perivascular drainage pathways Glymphatic system Meningeal lymphatic vessels, olfactory/cervical lymphatic drainage route, and their association with CSF circulation The connection among different components of the brain's lymphatic drainage system [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] The putamen, as a portion of the basal ganglia, has a similar drainage system as the whole brain, with structural differences in perivascular spaces compared to the cerebral cortex. [21]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Nerves
content: The putamen, situated in the striatal/dorsal portion of the basal ganglia, functions in harmony with the cortex through a complex cortico-basal ganglia network to perform and produce complex behaviors. It appears to be the coordination between separate functional channels and the integration across a function that directs coordinated behavior and can be modified by external and internal stimuli. [1] The 3 primary afferent input sources to the striatum are the cerebral cortex, the thalamus, and, primarily, dopaminergic cells of the brain stem. Accordingly, outputs from the striatum travel to the pallidum complex and the substantia nigra, pars reticulata, and pars compacta. [1]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Physiologic Variants
content: Volumetric changes of the putamen have been linked to different neurologic and psychiatric disorders. Researchers have conducted large imaging meta-analyses to establish the physiologic variation of the putamen, making it comparable to its pathologic condition and enabling determination of its physiological state. Almost all studies have shown that the volume of the putamen declines in both genders with aging. [3] [22] However, the effects of gender and hemispheric asymmetry remain controversial. [3] [22] [23]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Surgical Considerations
content: The putamen, a common structure affected by hypertensive cerebral hemorrhage, exhibits a wide range of presentations depending on the magnitude of the initial blood extravasation. [24] Despite the controversy, surgical evacuation of the intracerebral hemorrhage is a mainstay therapeutic approach to decompress the mass effect and also eliminate the cytotoxic edema resulting from the ischemia and the degraded blood products. [25] Current recommendations to remove putaminal bleed include a large-sized hematoma with life-threatening herniation, especially in young patients. [26] The other indication of removal of hematoma includes the presence of hemiparesis owing to the compression of the internal capsule from the hematoma that can be confirmed by the application of the MR tractography study (see Image. Coronal Section of Brain Through Anterior Commissure). [26]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Surgical Considerations
content: Different surgical approaches are chosen based on the hematoma size and position, the patient's hemodynamic stability, the underlying etiology, resource availability, and the surgeon's preference. [25] [27]  [28] For example, the putaminal hemorrhages associated with arteriovenous malformations make it a contraindication for endoscopic surgery. [29] Therefore, it necessitates changing from the endoscopic to the microscopic approach. [27] Traditionally, a craniotomy was the first-line surgical treatment, but due to its high mortality and morbidity rate, endoscopy, and most recently, navigation-guided or stereotactic aspiration have been the favored techniques. [26] Although less invasive, hematoma evacuation remains inefficient in endoscopy surgery owing to obscured visualization and limited or incomplete hemostasis. [25] [28] Therefore, a stainless-steel tube helps to guide the endoscope during the evacuation procedure. [28] Moreover, standard endoscopic techniques, precise targeting of lesions, noneloquent assessment with minimal brain retraction, and maintenance of optimal hemostasis are critical factors for eliminating postoperative complications. [25]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Surgical Considerations
content: Despite all the disagreements over the timing of surgery and the appropriate surgical approach (craniotomy, stereotactic, or endoscopic) for hematoma evacuation, the most important factor to keep in mind is fast decompression to control the intracranial pressure, not the complete evacuation. [29]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Clinical Significance
content: The putamen is a common site for hypertensive bleed as well as infarction. The corkscrew pattern of lenticulostriate vessels (increases intraluminal pressure), as well as the formation of Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm secondary to fibrinoid necrosis, predisposes to its rupture. [24] [30] On the contrary, lipohyalinosis and micro-atheroma formation result in infarction. [24] Bilateral putaminal hemorrhages, though rare, can occur in cases of bleeding disorders, methanol intoxication, metastatic lesions, and amyloid angiopathies. There can be a multispectral presentation in cases with small putaminal strokes, and these can be categorized as follows: Mixed motor and sensory Pure motor Pure sensory Ataxic hemiparesis Dysarthria with clumsy hands Hemiballism and hemichorea [24]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Clinical Significance
content: Aphasia can occur with a putaminal bleed in the dominant hemisphere, whereas spatial and hemineglect occur with right putaminal bleeds. [24] The presence of a conjugate eye deviation (CED) has been regarded as a poor prognostic marker in these bleeds. [31]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Clinical Significance
content: The putamen correlates with a broad spectrum of movement disorders and psychiatric diseases. The most well-known movement disorder related to the putamen is Parkinson disease, which is the result of dopamine depletion in the posterior putamen and presents with rigidity, tremor, ataxia, and impairment of balance. Changes in putamen volume are associated with a wide range of diseases. [22] While some disorders increase the volume of the putamen, including bipolar disorder, Tourette syndrome, attention-deficit-hyperactivity disorder, researchers have seen a decline in volume in major depressive disorder, Williams syndrome, autism, schizophrenia, and suicide attempters. [32] [33] [34] [35]    [36] [37] [38]  [39] Interestingly, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) prevents putaminal volume loss associated with normal aging. [40] It has also been documented that repetitive behaviors of OCD develop in the putaminal lesions. [41] Other pathologic conditions linked to dysfunction of the putamen include Huntington disease, Lewy body disorders, Alzheimer disease, Wilson disease, motor and cognitive impairment following putaminal hemorrhage, gait dysregulation following a stroke, and bilateral putaminal necrosis as a sequela of methanol toxicity. [42] [43] [44]

title: Neuroanatomy, Putamen -- Other Issues
content: Interesting findings regarding the involvement of the putamen in various physiological states: Studies have demonstrated that the total volume of the bilateral putamen in bilinguals is greater compared to that of monolingual individuals. A recent neuropsychological study evaluated the volumes of subcortical structures in relation to the ability to recognize facial expressions of emotion. The results elicited that the putamen volume inversely correlated with the recognition of the fearful face. The putamen, along with other brain regions, including the orbitofrontal cortices in the left and right hemispheres, is involved in recognizing one’s own infant versus other infants, demonstrating the significant role of striatal structures in maternal behavior and love. [8] [45] [46]
